clue.text: Face up to footballer's challenge

definitions.meaning: first meaning: to confront or deal with a problem head-on
second meaning: a footballer's attempt to win the ball from an opponent

explanation.walkthrough: A verb meaning confront and a noun from football share one word.
explanation.definitionFit: To deal with a problem squarely is to tackle it, and a sliding block for the ball is a tackle in football.

clue.text: Soldier holds up report with nothing in it

indicators.note: the nought is placed inside the reversed word
in a down answer, up means the word report is written bottom to top

parts.note: taken as written, the word to be turned round
zero looks like the letter O

explanation.surface: A soldier delays filing a report that turns out to be empty.
explanation.definitionFit: A trooper is a private soldier in a cavalry or armoured regiment.

clue.text: Unobstructed look at Uncle Arthur

indicators.note: looking at the words closely shows the answer sitting inside them

parts.note: the run of letters spans the end of the first name and the start of the second

explanation.surface: An invitation to take a good look at a relative named Arthur.
explanation.definitionFit: A clear path or view has nothing blocking it.

clue.text: Socialist unconscious of being ignored

parts.note: the left is the political wing that includes socialists
out cold means knocked unconscious

explanation.surface: A left-wing politician is oblivious to being snubbed.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone left out is excluded or overlooked, not included with the others.

clue.text: Her sin leads to a black eye

indicators.note: the letters of her sin lead on to a new word once rearranged

parts.note: taken as written: the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A moralising tale: a woman's sin ends with her being punched.
explanation.definitionFit: Shiner is informal slang for a bruised eye after a punch.

clue.text: Fish served to a Liberal in a small dwelling

indicators.note: the article and the party abbreviation go inside the small house

parts.note: a hut is a small simple house
taken as written

explanation.surface: A seafood supper is dished up to a Liberal politician in a cottage.
explanation.definitionFit: Halibut is a large flatfish of northern seas, eaten widely.

clue.text: Like Grieg, wearing no disguise

indicators.note: a disguise changes how something appears, so these letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written: the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: The composer Grieg appearing barefaced, without a costume.
explanation.definitionFit: Edvard Grieg was a composer from Norway, so the adjective of nationality fits him.

clue.text: Drive back with Prue in distress to college

indicators.note: being in distress is being upset, so the name's letters are disturbed

parts.note: taken as written: the name's letters are the ones rearranged
the LSE is the London School of Economics

explanation.surface: Fight off attackers while a tearful Prue heads to university.
explanation.definitionFit: To repulse an attack is to force the attackers to retreat.

clue.text: Run with dog awkwardly in stadium

indicators.note: doing something awkwardly means clumsily, so these letters come out jumbled

parts.note: taken as written, part of the letters rearranged
taken as written, the rest of the letters rearranged

explanation.surface: A dog lollops clumsily around a sports arena.
explanation.definitionFit: A football club's home stadium is commonly called its ground in Britain.

clue.text: Re-ordering of more red polony could make an easy buck or two

indicators.note: putting the letters of these words in a different order signals an anagram

parts.note: taken as written: all fifteen letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A deli shuffles its sausage stock and somehow turns a quick profit.
explanation.walkthrough: Polony is a smoked sausage, popular in Britain and South Africa. The idiom is British for payment for very little effort.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom describes cash earned for almost no work, so a buck or two gained easily.

clue.text: Iberian city left in holes

indicators.note: the word for left sits inside the two holes

parts.note: each hole is shaped like the letter O, so two holes give two Os
port is the nautical word for the left side of a ship

explanation.surface: A Spanish or Portuguese city has been abandoned in a sorry, hole-ridden state.
explanation.definitionFit: Oporto is the English name for Porto, Portugal's second city on the Iberian peninsula.

clue.text: Cracked lumber sent to LA for protection

indicators.note: wood that is cracked is broken up, so the letters of lumber are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written: the timber's letters are rearranged
taken as written

explanation.surface: Damaged timber is shipped off to Los Angeles to be used as a shield.
explanation.definitionFit: An umbrella shields from rain, and figuratively means any covering protection, as under the umbrella of an organisation.

clue.text: Stopped one blushing about a holiday

indicators.note: the colour word wraps around the break

parts.note: someone blushing goes red in the face
a rest is a break from work, much as a holiday is

explanation.surface: Someone red-faced on vacation is pulled up short.
explanation.definitionFit: Arrested means halted or checked, as in arrested development, as well as detained by police.

clue.text: Shut in, but having company in the end

indicators.note: the group is placed inside the word end

parts.note: taken as written, the word that encloses the group
a circle is a group of people sharing company or interests

explanation.surface: A prisoner who was locked up finally gets some company.
explanation.definitionFit: Encircled means surrounded on all sides, so hemmed or closed in.

clue.text: Powder room to let — I must go inside

indicators.note: says the letter I is placed within the two words before it

parts.note: taken as written, the words of a rental sign
taken as written

explanation.surface: A rental notice for a ladies' cloakroom, with a desperate plea from someone who needs it.
explanation.definitionFit: Powder room is a polite euphemism for a lavatory, especially a ladies' one.

clue.text: Calculator nearly makes a graduate swear

parts.note: taken as written
a BA is a Bachelor of Arts, a graduate's degree

indicators.note: only almost all of the word is used, so its last letter goes

parts.note: cuss is an informal word for swear

explanation.surface: A mathematics student nearly loses their temper over sums.
explanation.definitionFit: An abacus is a frame of beads on wires used for counting, an early calculating device.

clue.text: Was Garibaldi surprised to take it?

definitions.text: Was Garibaldi surprised to take it?

parts.note: reads as a question about the Italian general, but a Garibaldi is also a currant-filled British cookie
points to the idiom that takes the ... for something outrageous, which completes with the cookie

explanation.walkthrough: A Garibaldi is a flat British currant cookie; something that takes the biscuit is astonishingly outrageous.
explanation.definitionFit: The Garibaldi is one kind of this baked snack, and the idiom about surprise uses the same word.

clue.text: Lends grease not used for cultivation

definitions.note: a noun phrase in sense: the layer described as not cultivated

parts.note: in British informal use, to sub someone is to lend them money as an advance
oil is a greasy lubricant

explanation.surface: Someone hands out lubricant that will never touch farmland.
explanation.definitionFit: Subsoil is the earth beneath the topsoil, which ploughing and planting do not reach.

clue.text: Mockery for wearing a badge outside

indicators.note: the badge sits outside the other pieces, wrapping them

parts.note: taken as written, the word that wraps the others
in a garment means wearing it, as in in red
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone is teased for pinning a badge on the outside of their coat.
explanation.definitionFit: Badinage is playful, teasing banter, a light form of ridicule.

clue.text: The Chancellor's finances blossom and grow

parts.note: a bud is a flower before it opens
get means become, as in get older, a sense of grow

explanation.surface: The nation's economy flourishes and expands under the Chancellor.
explanation.walkthrough: The Chancellor of the Exchequer is Britain's finance minister, who presents the annual budget.
explanation.definitionFit: The budget is the government's annual statement of spending and taxation plans.

clue.text: Leonardo wants a lot of dancing about six

indicators.note: the shortened word goes around the numeral
most but not all of the word is used, so its tail is cut

parts.note: taken as written, before its last letters are cut
VI is six in Roman numerals

explanation.surface: Leonardo is keen on plenty of dancing around half a dozen times.
explanation.definitionFit: Leonardo da Vinci was the Italian Renaissance painter and inventor.

clue.text: Being energetic, vanish with a loaf

parts.note: go can mean disappear, as in the pain has gone
taken as written
loaf is British slang for head, from rhyming slang loaf of bread

explanation.surface: An energetic person disappears with a loaf of bread.
explanation.definitionFit: A go-ahead person or firm is enterprising and full of drive.

clue.text: A writer dead and put down

parts.note: taken as written
a scribe is one who writes or copies documents

explanation.surface: An obituary line: an author has died and been buried.
explanation.walkthrough: Put down here means attributed, as in put down to tiredness, not killed or buried.
explanation.definitionFit: To ascribe something is to credit or attribute it to a cause, the sense of put down to.

clue.text: Delinquent boy backs into motor vehicle

parts.note: a van is a small goods vehicle

indicators.note: the boy reverses, so his letters run backwards

parts.note: a lad is a boy

explanation.surface: A young lout reverses straight into a parked van.
explanation.definitionFit: A vandal is a destructive troublemaker, a kind of young offender who damages property.

clue.text: Hooters: noises from which one must escape

indicators.note: the letter for one has to get out of the word, so it is removed

parts.note: taken as written, the word one letter leaves
the Roman numeral I stands for one

explanation.surface: Car horns sound, and you need to get away from the racket.
explanation.definitionFit: Hooter is British slang for a nose, especially a large one.

clue.text: Wicked Nell wanting goose's plume to tease a person

indicators.note: a wicked act twists things, so these letters are reworked

parts.note: taken as written, part of the letters rearranged
taken as written, the rest of the letters rearranged

explanation.surface: Naughty Nell plucks a feather from a goose in order to tickle someone.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means to joke with somebody by telling them something untrue.

clue.text: Tight game, winks not allowed

indicators.note: the winks part is barred, so it is removed

parts.note: tiddlywinks is the game of flicking small discs into a cup
taken as written

explanation.surface: A close-fought match where winking at your opponent is banned.
explanation.walkthrough: Tight is the definition, meaning slightly drunk, not close.
explanation.definitionFit: Tiddly is British informal for a little drunk, the same slang sense as tight.

clue.text: Teacher to keep Edward behind, but forgot

indicators.note: the short form of Edward comes after the teacher

parts.note: Miss is how British schoolchildren address a female teacher
Ed is the short form of the name Edward

explanation.surface: A teacher means to give Edward a detention but it slips her mind.
explanation.definitionFit: To miss something can mean to fail to remember or overlook it, as in missed an appointment.
